title: URL shortener
tagline: Turn long links into short ones and redirect millions of clicks a day, fast.
govtech_note:
OGP runs go.gov.sg, the official government link shortener. Its public README describes Postgres for the short-to-long mappings with a read replica serving redirects, Redis for sessions, OTPs, click stats and hot links, and officers logging in with email OTP. Public reports give about 190M clicks (~2.1M a day) and 8.7M links as of Q3 2026.

A URL shortener is also a common GovTech TAP / intern and OGP intern take-home; a GovTech blog says it was once used as an interview exercise and later dropped. Expect follow-ups on who may create links, phishing targets and click analytics.
summary: Reads dominate: one link is created once and clicked thousands of times. So the design is a small write path that mints a unique key, and a very hot read path that answers GET /abc123 from cache in a millisecond and returns a 301/302 redirect.

functional: Create a short link for a long URL (optionally a custom alias)
Owner can edit or deactivate their links
nonfunctional: Redirect p99 under ~50 ms; reads are ~100× writes
Highly available: a dead redirect breaks every printed poster
Short keys must be unique and hard to guess

estimates.label: Redirect QPS (peak)
estimates.calc: × 20 when a link goes out in a national SMS blast

api.desc: Auth required. Returns {shortUrl}. 409 if alias taken.
Public. 302 to longUrl, 404 if unknown or deactivated.

steps.note: Visitor opens go.gov.sg/abc. DNS points at the CDN edge in Singapore.
Edge has no cached response for /abc (or it expired), so it forwards to any redirect replica behind the load balancer.
Service looks up abc in Redis: hit, ~1 ms.
Fire-and-forget a click event onto the queue. Never block the redirect on analytics.
Return 302 Found with Location: long URL. 302 (not 301) so browsers re-ask and edits take effect and clicks are counted.
Browser follows the redirect. Total server time: a few milliseconds.

flows.name: Redirect (cache miss)
flows.desc: First click after a cold start or eviction.

steps.note: Read the row from a Postgres read replica by primary key.
Write abc → URL back to Redis with a TTL (cache-aside). The next click is a hit.
Signed-in officer submits a long URL and an optional custom alias.
Check the target against a malicious-URL list. Government links are a phishing magnet.
INSERT with a unique constraint on alias. Random 7-char base62 key; on the rare collision, retry. Custom alias taken → 409.
Worker pulls click events in batches of hundreds.
Aggregate in memory, then one UPSERT per (alias, day). The DB sees a few writes a second instead of one per click.

deep.title: Generating the key
deep.html:
• Random base62, 7 chars + unique constraint: simple, unguessable, collisions astronomically rare at this scale. My default.
  • Counter → base62 (e.g. a DB sequence or ID ranges handed to each server): no collisions, but keys are sequential and guessable, so people can enumerate links.
  • Hash of the URL (MD5 → first 7 chars): same URL gives same key, but collisions need handling and different owners can't have separate links.

deep.title: 301 or 302?
deep.html: 301 is cached by browsers forever: fewer hits on you, but you lose click counts and can never change the target. 302/307 keeps every click flowing through you. Government links get edited (wrong form version, expired page) so I'd use 302 and let the CDN cache it for a short TTL.

deep.title: Abuse
deep.html: Restrict creation to verified government emails, scan targets on create and periodically (a safe page can turn malicious), rate-limit creation per user, and show an interstitial warning for external domains.

tradeoffs.why: A few GB fits easily on one Postgres primary, and the unique constraint gives free alias-collision safety. go.gov.sg's README describes exactly this, with a read replica for redirects. A key-value store (DynamoDB) is fine if you expect 100× growth.

tradeoffs.choice: Count clicks on the redirect path?
tradeoffs.why: A synchronous UPDATE per click turns a read-heavy system into a write-heavy one and puts the DB on the hot path.
Link popularity is very skewed; a small cache absorbs most traffic.

bottlenecks.issue: A link goes viral in an SMS blast to 5M residents
bottlenecks.fix: CDN caches the 302 for 60 s, Redis serves the rest, replicas autoscale. The DB never sees the spike.
Redirects fall back to read replicas (slower, still correct). Run Redis with a replica and failover.

followups.q: How do you stop someone guessing private links?
followups.a: Random (not sequential) keys with enough entropy: 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion, so guessing a live one is hopeless. Add rate limiting on 404s per IP.

followups.q: How would you support link expiry?
followups.a: Store expires_at; the redirect service checks it (cache TTL ≤ time to expiry). A nightly job marks expired rows inactive.

followups.q: What if two officers request the same custom alias at the same time?
followups.a: Both INSERT; the unique index lets exactly one win. The other gets a constraint error → return 409. No locks or read-then-write race.

quiz.q: Why put click counting behind a queue?
options: So the redirect never waits on a write and the DB sees batched writes
quiz.why: The hot path stays read-only; the worker turns 1,000 clicks into one UPSERT.

quiz.q: Which key scheme lets people enumerate other links?
quiz.why: Sequential IDs are predictable: abc1, abc2, abc3…

quiz.q: A link was printed on 2 million letters, then the target page moved. Which redirect status lets you fix it?
quiz.why: Browsers cache 301s indefinitely, so an edit never reaches people who clicked before. A 302 makes every click ask the service again.
